records.place: Mád, Tokaj, north east Hungary; the vineyard lies at Tarcal

wine.name: Royal Tokaji Mézes Mály 6 Puttonyos
wine.classification: Great First Growth, ranked above the first class in Tokaj's eighteenth century classification
wine.grapes: Furmint for the greater part, with Hárslevelű; some older vintages also held a little Sárga Muskotály, the yellow Muscat.
wine.sites: Mézes Mály, a warm slope above Tarcal whose loess topsoil, the house says, gives the wine its honeyed, blossom scented cast; the hill's name is recorded from the Middle Ages.
wine.making: Aszú berries, shrivelled by noble rot and picked one by one, soak for some two days in must that is already fermenting before they go to the press. The fermentation finishes in used casks of Zemplén oak, of three hundred and five hundred litres, where the wine matures for about two years in cellars the house dates to the thirteenth century.
wine.glass: Apricot, orange marmalade and honey, with a scent of blossom that the house puts down to the loess; dense and very sweet, with Furmint's high, saline acidity holding it upright to the end.
wine.ageing: Sweet and open from the day it is released, it lives for decades, its acidity holding the sugar in balance as the colour deepens towards amber.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius; leave the decanter aside; a small pour in a little white wine glass, with the dessert or as the dessert.

label.means: The sweet wine of noble rotted aszú berries steeped in must or wine; at least 120 grams of sugar a litre.
An optional mark since the 2013 vintage, kept for an Aszú of at least 150 grams of sugar a litre.
The house's words on later vintages, where older labels said 1st Growth, for the vineyard's historic rank.

records.table: Royal Tokaji draws its Mézes Mály 6 Puttonyos, an Aszú, from one historic vineyard at Tarcal, ranked above the first class in the eighteenth century. Furmint's bright acidity holds up its honey and apricot, and the house credits the loess with its scent of blossom.
records.story: Mézes Mály, whose name speaks of honey, is a hill at Tarcal recorded in the Middle Ages, far older than the house that bottles it, and Tokaj's eighteenth century surveys set it with its neighbour Szarvas above the first class. Through the communist decades the district's vines were worked by the state and its cooperatives, and the old vineyard names left the labels. In 1990, as Hungary left communism, a British wine writer and a winemaker from Denmark joined about sixty growers of Mád to found the company, among the first foreign ventures in Tokaj after the change. Its first wine, by its own account, was an Aszú of 1990 from the Betsek vineyard, and through its first decade it made Aszú alone, reviving the custom of naming the classified vineyards on the label: Betsek, Nyulászó, Szent Tamás and Mézes Mály. In 2010, its twentieth year, it opened a new winery at Mád, and later vintages of Mézes Mály, once labelled First Growth, carry the words Great First Growth. It reads Tokaj's old map of vineyards back into the glass, with the same Aszú method, one named site and the loess beneath it.

others.name: Szent Tamás Aszú 6 Puttonyos

others.name: Royal Tokaji Essencia

traps: Mézes Mály lies at Tarcal, not at Mád: the company is based at Mád but bottles vineyards of more than one village.
Puttonyos 3 and 4 were abolished from the 2013 vintage; every Aszú holds at least 120 grams of sugar a litre, and 6 Puttonyos marks at least 150.
Tokaj is the place and Tokaji the wine; Mézes Mály and Szarvas, both at Tarcal, were the two vineyards set above the first class.

It is the first wine the house releases each year
It is made of aszú berries alone, with no base wine

questions.q: Foreign partners and the growers of Mád founded The Royal Tokaji Wine Company together. When?
questions.exp: The company was founded in 1990 as Hungary left communism; 1737 is the royal decree that closed the Tokaj district, and 2010 the year of its new winery at Mád.

report: Searches for this record: six of the group's 35, two restricted to royal-tokaji.com, and one more on the Aszú rules (120 and 150 grams, eighteen months in oak) shared by the group; the one fetch tried (royal-tokaji.com) was refused, so the house's pages were read through search summaries only.

Mézes Mály lies at Tarcal, as the region record and Vinous have it; the library's holdings line for p-royal-tokaji puts it among the vineyards of Mád and its neighbours, which is loose rather than wrong.
The rank above the first class is dated 1730 by the house's importer, about 1700 by others and to the surveys of 1737 and 1772 by others again, so the record says only the eighteenth century.

The making (two days in fermenting must, Zemplén oak, two years and more, casks mostly of 500 litres) rests on the house's 2018 sheet and the importer's 2007 sheet; the cellars of the thirteenth century are the house's claim and are hedged.

The founders (a British wine writer, a winemaker called Danish by one source and Anglo Danish by Wine-Searcher, and a wine merchant) are living and described; sources give about sixty, sixty two (Fells) or sixty three growers, so the story says about sixty.

The first wine of 1990 from Betsek, the first decade of Aszú alone and the winery of 2010 rest on the house's own pages; the Codex's master question m-k3kcrfrz already names the living founders, which is the integrator's matter.

changed: wine.sites and story: Mézes Mály was a warm bowl on the northern edge of Tarcal whose name appears in records from the sixteenth century; it is now a warm slope above Tarcal whose hill is recorded from the Middle Ages, since a Tarcal estate's page on its sites and a Hungarian review give the Mézesmál hill in 1280 and 1411, and no source of this check placed it on the northern edge.

wine.making: the wine no longer matures for two years or more mostly in casks of about five hundred litres, but for about two years in used casks of Zemplén oak of three hundred and five hundred litres, as Decanter on the 2019 Aszús, the importer's sheets for 2008 and 2016 and the house's own word on its oak since 2010 give it.
wine.glass: the scent of dry dust is cut; the importer's and the house's notes credit the loess with honey and blossom only.

cards[1].back: the first wine is now named as the Betsek Aszú 5 Puttonyos of 1990, as the house's page for that wine and Decanter's first decade tasting give it; Decanter also confirms Aszú alone from 1990 to 1999 and about sixty growers.
open: The year of the classification that set Mézes Mály and Szarvas above the first class: 1700 in the importers' and a Napa paper's accounts, the 1730s and 1737 in others; the record keeps the eighteenth century, though 1700 is strictly the last year of the seventeenth.
The cellars of the thirteenth century are the house's claim and stay hedged; one importer says they were dug against the Turks, which would put them later.
Founded stays 1990, the library's year, with the house and Wine-Searcher; Berry Bros. and Rudd and one other give 1989, and one founder's account calls 1993 the first proper vintage.

records.place: Tolcsva, in the north of the Tokaj district, Hungary

wine.name: Oremus Tokaji Aszú 6 Puttonyos
wine.grapes: Furmint and Hárslevelű, with Zéta and Sárga Muskotály, Tokaj's yellow Muscat, in most vintages.
wine.sites: Parcels around Tolcsva in the north of the district, on volcanic rock and clay, and in the historic Oremus vineyard on a hill at Sátoraljaújhely that lent the estate its name.
wine.making: By the old measure, as the house describes it, six puttonyos, hods of about 25 kilograms of aszú berries, go to each 136 litre gönci barrel of must. The berries soak for a day or two until they swell, are gently pressed and ferment slowly for weeks in new Hungarian oak; the wine then ages two to three years in small barrels of 136 and 220 litres in cellars cut into volcanic rock, and rests in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Honey, candied orange peel and saffron over a hint of wild berries; silky and deeply sweet, with a sharp acidity that leaves the palate clean.
wine.ageing: Held back through its years in barrel and bottle, it drinks well once released, and a cool cellar will keep it for decades.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius; it needs no decanter; a small wine glass, alone at the end of the meal.

label.means: The estate's name, from the historic Oremus vineyard; oremus is Latin for let us pray.
Shrivelled, noble rotted berries soaked in must; never below 120 grams of sugar a litre.
Six hods of aszú berries to a gönci barrel in the old measure; by law at least 150 grams of sugar a litre.

records.table: Tokaj Oremus, the Tolcsva estate bought in 1993 by the family of Vega Sicilia, gives its Aszú 6 Puttonyos two to three years in small barrels in volcanic cellars. Honey, candied orange and saffron meet sharp acidity, and the wine rests in bottle as well before release.
records.story: Long before it named an estate, Oremus, Latin for let us pray, named a vineyard on a hill at Sátoraljaújhely in the north of Tokaj, and legend holds that there, about 1630, a Calvinist preacher at the court of the Rákóczi princes made the first Aszú. Historians treat the tale as legend: aszú is named in a document of 1571, and the preacher's own long chronicle says nothing of Aszú. The house holds that the Oremus vineyard was ranked of the first class, Primae Classis, in 1772. After communism, in 1993, the Álvarez family, who had bought Vega Sicilia in Ribera del Duero in 1982, bought an estate at Tolcsva and set up Tokaj Oremus, one of several ventures from abroad that put money into the district in those years. In 1999 a new winery rose at Tolcsva, joined to a maze of cellars the house traces to the thirteenth century, and around 2000 it began its dry Furmint, Mandolás. The Aszú is made the old way, by the puttony and the gönci barrel, and held long before release, in the manner of Vega Sicilia. Two answers meet in it: one family in Spain and in Tokaj, and a vineyard whose name carries the founding legend of Aszú.

others.name: Mandolás
others.note: Dry Furmint named for the estate's Mandulás hill at Tolcsva, one of the early dry wines of modern Tokaj.

others.name: Oremus Tokaji Aszú 5 Puttonyos
others.note: The same method with less sugar, also aged long in the cellar before release.

others.name: Oremus Eszencia
others.note: The syrup that runs freely from the aszú berries, fermenting for years to only a few degrees of alcohol.

traps: Oremus is also the old name of the grape Zéta, a cross of Furmint and Bouvier renamed in 1999: grape, vineyard and estate are three different things.
Oremus was bought in 1993 by the family that had bought Vega Sicilia, in Ribera del Duero, in 1982: one family, two countries, two unrelated answers.
The first Aszú of about 1630 is a legend, not a record: aszú is named in a document of 1571.

cards.front: Tokaj Oremus: what is Mandolás, and what is it named for?
cards.back: The estate's dry Furmint, begun around 2000 and named for its Mandulás hill at Tolcsva.

cards.front: Which grape of Tokaj went by the name Oremus until 1999?
cards.back: Zéta, a cross of Furmint and Bouvier, quick to take noble rot.

questions.q: A guest asks how Tokaj Oremus makes its Aszú 6 Puttonyos. Which description matches what the house itself says?
opts: Aszú berries soaked a day or two in must, then aged in small barrels
Grapes dried on mats, then aged in large chestnut casks
Frozen grapes pressed, then aged in steel tanks
Grapes raisined on the vine, then aged in bottle alone
questions.exp: The house soaks the aszú berries a day or two in must and ages the wine two to three years in small barrels; grapes dried on mats make a passito, not an Aszú.

questions.q: Legend says a preacher made the first Aszú from the Oremus vineyard about 1630. In which earlier year is aszú named in a document?
questions.exp: Historians found aszú named in a document of 1571, so the tale of about 1630 is a legend; in 1737 a royal decree closed the district, and 1772 is the house's date for the vineyard's first class rank.

report: Searches for this record: nine of the group's 35, two restricted to Vega Sicilia's domain (temposvegasicilia.com) and two spent in vain on the preacher's dates; no fetch tried on it.
Founded is 1993, the year the Álvarez family bought the estate and set up Tokaj Oremus (Michelin Guide, Wine-Searcher and the house); the library gives no year.

The preacher of the legend is described, not named: his dates (1576 to 1633) were found in one study only; the legend's date is 1630 in most accounts, 1631 and 1650 in others, so the record says about 1630.

That the legend is unfounded and that aszú is named in 1571 rests on a study in Történelmi Szemle and on Wines of Hungary and Hello Hungary; the Oremus vineyard's Primae Classis of 1772 is the house's claim and is hedged.
Mandolás is dated 2000 in one Vega Sicilia sheet and 2001 in another, so the story says around 2000; the house's claim that it was Tokaj's first dry wine is left out.

The grapes vary by vintage: the 2005 sheet names Furmint and Hárslevelű only, later sheets add Zéta and Sárga Muskotály; Zéta's old name Oremus rests on the region record, Wikipedia and Wines of Hungary.
The library lists only the 5 Puttonyos among the house's wines; the plan's 6 Puttonyos is the richer Aszú of the same method, and no swap is proposed.

changed: wine.making, cards[0].back, questions[0].opts[0] and exp: the berries soak a day or two until they swell, no longer two days, since three merchants' sheets of the house's Aszú 6 give twelve to twenty four hours or a day or two; the six puttonyos of 25 kilograms to a gönci of 136 litres and the two to three years in barrels of 136 and 220 litres are confirmed.
wine.sites: rhyolite and clay becomes volcanic rock and clay, since the estate's Petrács vineyard at Tolcsva is andesite by Berry Bros. and Rudd.

story: the preacher's long chronicle no longer barely mentions wine; it says nothing of Aszú, as Hello Hungary gives his great work of 1624, beside the study in Történelmi Szemle that calls the legend unfounded; aszú in the Garay inventory of 1571 is confirmed.
others[0].note: Mandolás is named for the estate's Mandulás hill at Tolcsva and is no longer said to come from a vineyard planted to Furmint alone, which no source of this check gave.
open: The Oremus vineyard's first class rank of 1772 is the house's claim and stays hedged; no independent source was found.
The estate's plot named Oremus appears on its tokaj.hu listing; that it lies on the Várhegy at Sátoraljaújhely rests on the vineyard's name and the study, not on a page of the estate.
The cellars of the thirteenth century are the house's claim; other accounts say the twelfth or the sixteenth.

records.place: Mezőzombor, at the southern edge of the Tokaj hills, Hungary

wine.name: Disznókő Tokaji Aszú 6 Puttonyos
wine.classification: From vineyards ranked first class in the eighteenth century, as the estate presents them
wine.grapes: Furmint alone for the aszú berries in the sheets of 2016 and 2019, steeped in a base wine of Furmint and Hárslevelű.
wine.sites: One unbroken tract of vines at Mezőzombor, named for the wild boar stone, a large volcanic rock at its heart; its first class sites include Disznókő, Hangács and Lajos, and the vineyard is recorded from 1413.
wine.making: Most of the aszú berries are steeped whole for about two days in fermenting must, the rest crushed and soaked for half a day, then pressed. The lots are kept apart and aged for about two years in barrels of 225 litres, mostly used, with a little new Hungarian oak, before they are blended.
wine.glass: Ripe apricot, peach and quince over acacia honey and a touch of sandalwood; unctuous and lavishly sweet, yet fresh, with clean, lifted acidity and a long finish touched with green spice.
wine.ageing: Ready to drink on release, as the estate says, yet able to keep for thirty years and more on the strength of its acidity.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius, or 11 to 13 as the estate itself suggests; there is nothing to decant; a small white wine glass.

label.means: Wild boar stone: the vineyard's name, from a large volcanic rock at its heart.
Of Tokaj: the suffix i turns the place into the name of its wine.
An Aszú of at least 150 grams of sugar a litre; the puttonyos figure is optional.

records.table: Named for the wild boar stone in its vineyard, the Mezőzombor estate of Disznókő steeps Furmint berries two days in fermenting must for its Aszú 6 Puttonyos. Apricot, peach and acacia honey come with clean, lifted acidity.
records.story: Records of 1413 already name the vineyard Disznókő, the wild boar stone, a name taken from a large volcanic rock at its heart or, some geographers say, from the shape of its hill. In a survey of Tokaj's vineyards drawn up in 1732, by the estate's account, its slopes were ranked first class. Under communism the vines were farmed intensively, and by 1992 they were in poor shape. That year AXA Millésimes, the wine arm of the French insurer, bought the property, a plain sign of the foreign money that reopened Tokaj after 1989. Replanting began in 1994, at a much higher density, with better oriented rows and modern trellising, and in 1995 a new winery designed by a Hungarian architect was built, its cellar cut about ten metres into the rhyolite. The estate keeps its lots apart in barrel and blends them only after about two years, and it later bottled the Kapi parcel as an Aszú of its own. Asked how foreign capital rebuilt Tokaj, a sommelier can answer with Disznókő, one old vineyard replanted and made anew.

others.name: Disznókő Kapi Vineyard Tokaji Aszú 6 Puttonyos
others.note: Aszú of the Kapi parcel alone, the estate's single vineyard bottling.

others.name: Disznókő Tokaji Late Harvest
others.note: A lighter sweet wine below Aszú, made without the steeping of aszú berries.

others.name: Disznókő Tokaji Száraz Szamorodni
others.note: A dry wine of whole bunches with their botrytised berries, as they come.

traps: Late Harvest and Szamorodni are not Aszú: only Aszú steeps selected aszú berries in must or wine.
Disznókő is a single vineyard estate at Mezőzombor, not a village of Tokaj.
Sárga Muskotály is a permitted grape of Tokaj, so a Muscat note does not rule out a Tokaji, though Disznókő's recent Aszú berries are Furmint alone.

cards.back: Wild boar stone, from a large volcanic rock at the heart of the vineyard, or from the shape of the hill, as some say.

cards.front: Disznókő: what began in 1994, two years after the estate changed hands?

questions.q: How does Disznókő steep the aszú berries for its Aszú 6 Puttonyos, by the estate's own sheet?
opts: Mostly whole, for about two days in fermenting must
Crushed, for about two weeks in finished dry wine
Whole, for about a month in grape spirit
Not at all: the berries are pressed straight away
questions.exp: Most of the berries steep whole for about two days in fermenting must and the rest, crushed, for about half a day; berries soaked in grape spirit would make no Aszú.

report: Searches for this record: four of the group's 35, all restricted to disznoko.hu and its importer's domain; no fetch tried on it.
The plan's why says a first growth of 1772; the estate's own history ties its first class rank to a survey drawn up in 1732, so the record follows the estate and leaves 1772 out.

The plan's boar shaped rock: the estate says the name comes from a large volcanic rock at the heart of the vineyard, or by some geographers from the hill's shape, so the record does not call the rock boar shaped.

The library's grapes for the flagship (Furmint, Hárslevelű and Sárga Muskotály) do not match the estate's sheets for 2016 and 2019, which give Furmint alone for the aszú berries and Furmint with Hárslevelű for the base wine; the record follows the sheets, and Zéta appears only in the estate's Sárga Borház and Dorgó wines.
The estate suggests serving at 11 to 13 degrees Celsius; the record keeps the Codex's 6 to 8 for Tokaji, for the integrator to weigh.
The author of the survey of 1732 and the architect of the winery of 1995 are described, not named, for want of their dates in two sources.

That the vines were a state farm before 1992 rests on the library's holdings line and the estate's poor shape at purchase; the estate itself only contrasts its wines with those of the communist years.

changed: wine.making and story: the twenty to thirty lots, found in no source of this check, are cut, and two years and more becomes about two years, as the estate's sheets for 2017 and 2019 give it; the whole berries for about two days, the crushed share for about twelve hours and the barrels of 225 litres with a little new oak are confirmed.
wine.serve: cold enough to show the acidity is cut, and the estate's own 11 to 13 degrees Celsius, from its sheet for 2017, now stands beside the Codex's 6 to 8.

story: the noble families who held the vineyard for centuries are cut, absent from the estate's history page in this check; the state farm becomes vines farmed intensively, the estate's own words for the years before 1992; the prize winning architect becomes a Hungarian architect.
questions[0].exp: about seven tenths of the berries becomes most of them, since the whole share runs from about two fifths to about two thirds across the estate's sheets.
open: The serving temperature: the estate's 11 to 13 degrees Celsius against the Codex's 6 to 8 for sweet whites; both stand in the serve, for the integrator.
The first class rank of 1732 is the estate's account of János Matolai's survey; no source outside the estate was found in this check.
The state farm of the library's holdings line is not on the estate's page, which speaks only of intensive cultivation before 1992.

wine.name: Szepsy Szent Tamás Furmint
wine.classification: A first class vineyard of Mád in Tokaj's eighteenth century classification
wine.grapes: Furmint, the grape the label names.
wine.sites: Szent Tamás, Saint Thomas, a large vineyard hill at the edge of Mád, on red clay over rhyolite tuff and zeolite.
wine.making: The vines are kept to very low yields and the grapes picked for a dry wine of this one vineyard alone. It ferments to dryness in Hungarian oak barrels of about three hundred litres, some of them new, and rests on its lees for some months before bottling, with no sweetness and no puttonyos mark.
wine.glass: Smoke, lime peel and chalk over green apple and a salty, stony core; dense and taut, with Furmint's high, firm acidity and a saline length.
wine.ageing: Reserved when young, it broadens over several years in bottle, and its acidity lets it keep for many years.
wine.serve: 11 to 13 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour if it seems closed; a large, Burgundy shaped white wine glass.

label.means: A varietal wine of the Tokaj appellation; a dry Furmint carries no puttonyos and no Aszú.
Saint Thomas: the vineyard, a first class slope at the edge of Mád.

records.table: Szepsy's Szent Tamás Furmint is a dry Tokaji from one first class slope at Mád, on red clay and volcanic rock. Smoke, lime and salt sit on searing acidity, so pour it a little cool, in a large glass, as you would a white Burgundy.
records.story: The family has made wine in Tokaj since the sixteenth century, by its own account, and links its line to a Calvinist preacher of the Rákóczi court whose name it shares, whom legend credits with the first Aszú about 1630, though the word aszú is already written down in 1571. In the communist years the head of the family tended vines of his own at Mád and delivered the grapes to the state, and in 1990 he took a leading part in founding the Royal Tokaji company with the growers of Mád. In 2000 he fermented the Furmint of Mád's Úrágya vineyard dry, a wine many accounts credit with setting off the movement towards dry single vineyard Furmint. The family's own label followed with dry Furmints of single vineyards, Szent Tamás among them, a slope ranked first class in the eighteenth century, beside Aszú made only when the year allows. Where Tokaj had been known for sweet wine alone, these bottles showed that its volcanic slopes could give dry whites of weight and long life, and other growers of Mád followed. For a sommelier, Szent Tamás is the bottle to open when a guest believes Tokaji must be sweet.

others.name: Szepsy Urbán Furmint
others.note: Dry Furmint from the Urbán vineyard, another classified site of Mád, stonier and tighter.

others.name: Szepsy Tokaji Aszú 6 Puttonyos
others.note: Made in small amounts and only in years that allow it.

traps: Tokaji on a label does not mean sweet: Szepsy's Szent Tamás is a dry white, as much a Tokaji as any Aszú.
Szent Tamás names a vineyard of Mád and also a separate winery of the village; Royal Tokaji, Szepsy and others bottle the vineyard, so read the name of the house.
Furmint's high acidity and smoky weight make it a blind tasting decoy for Chenin Blanc and dry Riesling.

cards.front: Szepsy Szent Tamás: what does the vineyard's name mean, and where does it lie?
cards.back: Saint Thomas; a large first class vineyard hill at the edge of Mád, on red clay over rhyolite tuff and zeolite.

cards.front: Szepsy: since when has the family made wine in Tokaj, by its own account?
cards.back: Since the sixteenth century, around the time aszú first appears in the records.

questions.q: A guest orders Szepsy's Szent Tamás Furmint expecting a sweet Tokaji. What do you tell the guest?
opts: It is a dry Furmint from one first class vineyard
It is an Aszú of six puttonyos from Mád
It is a late harvest wine with light sweetness
It is a Szamorodni aged under a veil of yeast
questions.exp: Szent Tamás is a dry single vineyard Furmint, so it carries no puttonyos; an Aszú or a late harvest wine would be sweet, and a Szamorodni would say so on the label.

questions.q: Which vintage of the Úrágya vineyard's Furmint, fermented dry by the head of the Szepsy family, do many accounts credit with setting off Tokaj's dry Furmint movement?
questions.exp: The Úrágya Furmint of 2000; 1990 is the year Royal Tokaji was founded with the growers of Mád, 1993 the year Oremus was set up at Tolcsva, and 2013 the year the Aszú rules changed.

report: Searches for this record: seven of the group's 35, two restricted to szepsy.hu, which gave one gallery page only; no fetch tried on it.
Founded is left empty, as in the library: the family dates its winemaking to the sixteenth century and no source gave a founding year for the estate.

The head of the family is living and never named; the people.json entry covers him, and the record says the head of the family. The partner and the estate of the dry wine of 2000 (Királyudvar, owned by a living man) are said as another Tokaj estate, since Királyudvar stands at Tarcal though the Úrágya vineyard is at Mád.

The fermentation vessel is not settled: the library says barrel fermented and one importer listing says fermentation in wooden barrels, another listing of the same importer says steel; the making says only some months in wooden barrels. The site (south facing, by the road into Mád, red clay with volcanic rock) rests on Royal Tokaji's page for its own Szent Tamás wine and the region record.

The family's link to the preacher of the legend is the family's own claim, called possible by one other source, and it is hedged; the preacher is described, not named, since his dates were found in one study only.

Two pages that date the family's first own label dry Furmint to 2003 could not be cited, since their addresses name a living person, and they disagree on the vineyard (Úrágya or Szent Tamás); the story gives no date for it.

The head of the family leading the growers of Mád into Royal Tokaji in 1990 rests on an article hosted on royal-tokaji.com and the Codex's master question m-k3kcrfrz, which cites nothing; Fells and Wine-Searcher name the investors but not him, so the story hedges it as Royal Tokaji's account and no card or question asks it.

changed: wine.sites and cards[0].back: Szent Tamás was a steep south facing slope beside the road into the village; it is now a large vineyard hill at the edge of Mád on red clay over rhyolite tuff and zeolite, since no source gave a south face (Royal Tokaji's own Szent Tamás comes from a west facing flank and another grower's parcel faces south west) and the road was in no source of this check.

wine.making: some months in wooden barrels becomes fermented dry in Hungarian oak barrels of about three hundred litres, some new, then some months on the lees, as two merchants' sheets for the wine agree; whether the yeasts are native or added is left out, since the sheets differ.

story: the head of the family no longer went on making fine wine through the communist decades; he tended vines of his own and delivered the grapes to the state, as two accounts give it; and in 1990 he took a leading part in founding Royal Tokaji (its manager in one account, a founding investor and a driving force in others), no longer led the growers of Mád.

story and questions[1]: the Úrágya Furmint of 2000 is no longer said to be made for another Tokaj estate, since Falstaff calls Úrágya his newly bought vineyard while Decanter places the wine at Királyudvar; it is credited with setting off the dry Furmint movement, no longer treated as the start of modern dry Tokaji, since Falstaff says it was not the first dry Furmint of Tokaj; the question's explanation now places 1993 too.
others[0].note: a second classified site becomes another classified site of Mád, so it cannot be read as second class.
traps[1]: Szent Tamás is no longer said to be no producer, since a winery of Mád is called Szent Tamás; the trap now says the name is both.
open: Whose estate the dry Úrágya of 2000 was made for: Falstaff (his own new vineyard) against Decanter (Királyudvar, where he worked then).
The first class rank of Szent Tamás rests on Royal Tokaji's labels and a grower's note; the record gives the eighteenth century as for the other vineyards.
The family's descent from the preacher of the legend is its own claim and stays hedged.

records.place: Tokaj town, where the Bodrog meets the Tisza, Tokaj, Hungary

wine.name: Dobogó Tokaji Aszú 6 Puttonyos
wine.grapes: Mostly Furmint, with Hárslevelű and a little Sárga Muskotály, or yellow Muscat, as the vineyards are planted.
wine.sites: Volcanic vineyards of Mád, Betsek, Szent Tamás and Úrágya among them; the cellar lies in the centre of Tokaj town.
wine.making: The base wine is the house's own late harvest wine, Mylitta, from shrivelled, partly botrytised grapes. A kilo of aszú berries goes to each litre of it, and the berries soak for about a day before pressing, which sets off a second fermentation. Two to three years in oak casks follow, then about three more in bottle in the cellar.
wine.glass: Dates, mango and dried apricot over orange blossom and orange peel, with a hint of jasmine tea; rich and sweet, bright acidity balancing it to a clean end.
wine.ageing: Five or six years in cask and bottle pass before it leaves the cellar; it is ready to pour then, and in a cool cellar it lasts for decades.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius, straight from the bottle with no decanting; a small glass, for a small measure.

label.means: The house's name, said to recall the beat of horses' hooves on cobbles as carts came home.
Of Tokaj, the district rather than the town: aszú berries steeped in a base wine, at least 120 grams of sugar a litre.
The richer of the two optional marks on an Aszú, at least 150 grams of sugar a litre.

records.table: Founded in 1995 by the family of the Unicum liqueur, Dobogó is a small house in Tokaj town. For its Aszú 6 Puttonyos, rich in dates, apricot and orange peel, the house steeps aszú berries in its own late harvest wine, then rests it for years in cask and bottle.
records.story: The Zwack family made Unicum, the herbal liqueur, in Pest from 1840. In 1948 the communist state nationalised the business, and the family left Hungary, taking the recipe with them. The head of the family came home in 1988, a year before communism fell, and soon won the firm back. In 1995 his daughter founded Dobogó, a small winery in a house said to date from 1869, in the centre of Tokaj town; its name, the house says, recalls the beat of horses' hooves on the cobbles as the carts came home from the vineyards. The grapes come from vineyards of Mád: Betsek, Szent Tamás and Úrágya. In 2003 a winemaker joined the founder as partner, and since then, by the house's account, at least a barrel of 6 Puttonyos Aszú has been made in every vintage. The house builds its Aszú on its own late harvest wine, Mylitta, rather than on a dry base, and gives it years in cask and bottle before release. Beside the sweet wines it makes dry Furmint of single vineyards such as Úrágya. Dobogó is the reminder that Tokaj's revival was not only the work of large foreign companies, for a Hungarian family, home from exile, built a small house around the classic Aszú.

others.name: Dobogó Mylitta
others.note: The late harvest wine of partly botrytised grapes, aged a year for freshness, which is also the base of the Aszú.

others.name: Dobogó Úrágya Tokaji Furmint
others.note: A dry single vineyard Furmint from vines planted in the early 2000s at the western edge of Mád.

traps: Mylitta is a late harvest wine, not an Aszú: it carries no puttonyos figure, though it is the base wine of the house's Aszú.
Tokaj names both the town where Dobogó stands and the whole district; Tokaji on the label means of the district, not of the town alone.
Dobogó was founded in 1995 by a Hungarian family, the Zwacks of Unicum, not by one of the foreign companies of the early 1990s.

report: Searches for this record: six of the group's 35, two restricted to dobogo.hu and the importer's domain; no fetch tried on it.

The plan's why says the house dates from 1869; no source found it, while the house, bor.hu, Vinissimus and Decanter give the founding of 1995, so 1869 is left out and the plan's why should be read again.

The founder and the winemaker partner of 2003 are living and are not named (Izabella Zwack and Attila Domokos, for people.json); the founder's father is described, since the story need not name him, though Wikipedia and Portfolio give his dates.

Unicum from 1840, the nationalisation of 1948, the return of 1988 and the firm won back in 1991 or 1992 (sources differ, so the early 1990s) rest on Wikipedia and others; the founder as his daughter on Decanter.
The house says it has made at least a barrel of 6 Puttonyos Aszú in every vintage since 2003, while its UK importer says only in the best vintages; the story gives the house's account, hedged.
The house's soak is about a day (24 hours on its Hungarian page, one night on the importer's), and the cask time two to three years with three more in bottle in both.

Dobogó is a small house that a guest may not know; if the checker wants a wider name, Hétszőlő or Királyudvar of Tarcal would serve, but no swap is pressed: Dobogó is well documented and its Aszú is its flagship.

changed: wine.sites and story: first class vineyards of Mád and Tállya, Betsek among them, become vineyards of Mád, Betsek, Szent Tamás and Úrágya, as two merchants' pages list them; Tállya is in no source of this check, and Falstaff says Úrágya was never ranked for sweet wine, so first class is cut.
wine.label[1]: Pincészet, the winery's Hungarian name that the label may not print, gives way to Tokaji Aszú.

story: Unicum was made in Pest, not Budapest, from 1840, since Buda and Pest were joined only in 1873; the firm was soon won back after the return of 1988, no longer in the early 1990s, since accounts give 1989 and 1992; and the winery stands in a house said to date from 1869, which an importer's sheet and a merchant's account give, with the house's own page speaking of a cellar of a hundred and fifty years: this is the year the plan's why read as a founding.
cards[1].back: won back as communism ended, for the same reason.
questions[1].opts: Pálinka, the fruit brandy, gives way to Dreher, the Budapest beer, since the Zwack firm also sells fruit brandies, which made a second answer arguable.
open: The house of 1869 rests on two secondary accounts that may share an importer's wording, and is hedged as said to date.

The making (Mylitta as the base, a kilo of berries to the litre, about a day of soaking, two to three years in cask and about three in bottle) is the house's own account with its importer; no independent source was found.
Tállya, in the author's sources only, is cut until a second source places the house's vines there.
